similar_scenes.name: Digital Underground y KMEL
similar_scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
similar_scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
similar_scenes.desc: Mientras Public Enemy y N.W.A se disputaban la conciencia del hip hop, Shock G (Gregory Jacobs), Chopmaster J y Kenny K formaron en 1987 Digital Underground, un grupo excéntrico devoto de Parliament-Funkadelic que absorbió a Raw Fusion (Money-B, DJ Fuze). KMEL, la emisora pop de Keith Naftaly, cambió el Top 40 por hip hop, R&B, reggae y house, rompió a Hammer, Vanilla Ice o DJ Quik e inventó el Summer Jam. Tras «Underwater Rimes», Tommy Boy publicó Sex Packets (1990): «The Humpty Dance» de su alter ego Humpty Hump los hizo estrellas pop, con «Doowutchyalike» y «Freaks of the Industry». Precursores del G-funk de Dr. Dre y trampolín de Tupac. Shock G murió en 2021.

similar_scenes.name: Rap afrocéntrico y P-Funk hip hop
similar_scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
similar_scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
similar_scenes.desc: Grupos neoyorquinos hablaban de orgullo africano, conciencia histórica y respeto a la mujer sobre samples de funk: los Jungle Brothers («Black Woman»), Queen Latifah («Ladies First»), De La Soul con 3 Feet High and Rising (1989) y X-Clan, guerreros tribales del Este que daban un «Funkin’ Lesson». Su productor Prince Paul llevaba al sampleo la estética de P-Funk: sketches, chistes internos y collages. Llegó una espiritualidad funky que cuestionaba la iglesia negra (KRS-One, Kam, el «Earthbound» de X-Clan con su «Funk upon a time»). La nación hip hop se reconoció heredera del funk: Digital Underground («Sons of the P», con Clinton; Shock G: «sobre todo necesitamos el funk»), James Brown en el vídeo de «2 Legit 2 Quit», Clinton y Bootsy con Ice Cube en «Bop Gun», Dr. Dre montando la Nave Nodriza en «Let Me Ride». Los viejos maestros pasaban la tradición a una juventud abandonada por sus líderes.

podcast.title: Early Digital Glitches in MP3 Compression
podcast.body: Initial efforts to develop MP3 compression were plagued by digital glitches that severely compromised audio quality, making early compressed tracks sound poor. Engineers dedicated substantial time and effort to resolve these technical issues and refine the algorithms. "Early attempts were plagued by digital glitches that made things sound awful."

srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: High-Resolution Audio Devices
podcast.body: There have been and continue to be attempts to persuade the public to buy dedicated music devices capable of playing high-resolution audio, which offers sound quality superior to that of a compact disc. However, convincing consumers to carry an additional device alongside their mobile phones has proven challenging, as demonstrated by the limited success of products like the Pono music player. "And at the other end, there have been and continue to be attempts at getting the public to purchase dedicated music devices that play high-resolution audio, which is digital music recorded at better than CD quality."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2

podcast.title: MP3 as a Music Sharing Medium
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, as internet usage increased, MP3s became an effective format for sharing music, even over slow dial-up modems. This ease of distribution prompted the recorded music industry's first major concerns regarding digital piracy. "In the middle 90s, with the internet starting to catch on, MP3's proved great for sharing music, even through clunky old dial-up modems."
